title: A film is still frames shown fast
description: A film is a series of still photographs projected in rapid succession, fast enough to look like smooth movement.

facts.text: Britannica defines a film as a series of still photographs projected onto a screen in rapid succession, giving the illusion of smooth, continuous movement.

title: From photographs to projection to television
description: Moving pictures grew from sequence photographs (1878) to films projected for a paying audience (1895), then to television, which delivers moving images electronically.

facts.text: In 1878 Eadweard Muybridge photographed a galloping horse with a row of cameras, a step from still photography toward motion pictures.
On December 28, 1895, the Lumière brothers projected films for a paying audience at the Grand Café in Paris.
Television delivers moving images and sound electronically from a source to a receiver; in 1928 General Electric began regular experimental television broadcasts in the United States.

title: The crafts that make a film
description: Film draws on nearly every other art plus technical skills: screenwriting, directing, acting, cinematography, design, music, sound and editing.

facts.text: Film requires contributions from nearly all the other arts as well as countless technical skills, such as sound recording, photography and optics.
Film developed as a means of artistic expression in acting, directing, screenwriting, cinematography, costume and set design, and music.
Editing is trimming and piecing together lengths of film into a complete motion picture; the editor judges how long each shot should last.

title: Apparent motion: the brain supplies the movement
description: Wertheimer's phi phenomenon and beta movement show the brain sees motion between still images shown in quick succession; to the visual system, film motion is like real motion.

facts.text: Psychologist Max Wertheimer described the phi phenomenon in 1912; he reportedly noticed it in 1910 when two alternating railway signal lights looked like one light in motion.
Beta movement occurs when a series of still images shows an object in a slightly different position in each image, and viewers see the object move.
The phi phenomenon and beta movement explain how animation, film and electronic displays create the illusion of continuous motion from a sequence of still images.
The visual system seemingly cannot tell the short-range apparent motion in a motion picture from real motion.

title: Persistence of vision: the older, oversimplified story
description: The claim that images linger on the retina and blend is an inadequate explanation of film motion; researchers separate flicker fusion from apparent motion.

facts.text: Persistence of vision, the idea that each image lingers on the retina and blends with the next, recurred in film writing for almost a century but is an inadequate explanation of apparent motion; blended images would only superimpose.
Perceptual psychology separates two effects in film: flicker fusion, which makes flickering light look steady, and apparent motion, which makes successive images look like movement.

title: Frame rates, from hand cranks to 24
description: A frame rate counts frames per second. The brain needs more than about 15; silent cameras were hand-cranked at 16 to 18 on average, and sound fixed the standard at 24 in 1927.

facts.text: The brain perceives continuous movement from a succession of still images exposed at a rate above 15 frames per second.
Silent-film cameras were mainly hand-cranked, at rates averaging 16 to 18 frames per second.
Silent films were photographed and projected at widely varying speeds.
Sound made a standard frame rate necessary, and in 1927 the speed was standardized at 24 frames per second, or 90 feet per minute for 35 mm film.
Cameras were motorized in 1929 to run at an even speed of 24 frames per second so sound stayed in sync.

title: Shooting speed versus showing speed
description: Film must be projected at the speed it was shot; project it faster and the action speeds up, shoot it faster and it plays in slow motion.

facts.text: To look natural, film must be projected at the speed it was shot: action filmed at 12 frames per second and projected at 24 plays twice as fast, and action filmed at 36 or more frames per second looks slow at 24.

title: Muybridge's galloping horse
description: Hired by Leland Stanford, Muybridge used a row of 12 thread-triggered cameras in 1878 to show a galloping horse lifts all four hooves at once, legs tucked under.

facts.text: Railroad magnate Leland Stanford hired photographer Eadweard Muybridge to prove that at one moment in its gallop a horse has all four legs off the ground.
On June 19, 1878, at Stanford's Palo Alto track, Muybridge photographed the mare Sallie Gardner galloping past a row of 12 cameras.
The camera shutters were released as the horse broke threads attached to them.
The photos showed a galloping horse with all four hooves off the ground at once, legs tucked under its body, not stretched out front and back as painters had shown.

title: The zoopraxiscope: photos projected in motion
description: Muybridge's zoopraxiscope projected his sequence images in rapid succession, a predecessor of cinema, but each sequence needed many cameras.

facts.text: Muybridge developed the zoopraxiscope, a lantern that projected images in rapid succession onto a screen and an important predecessor of cinema.

Muybridge's projected sequences came from multiple cameras; a camera invented in Edison's lab that recorded successive images by itself was more practical and influenced all later motion picture devices.

title: The Kinetoscope, a one-viewer movie cabinet
description: Developed largely by W. K. L. Dickson in Edison's lab, the Kinetoscope let one person at a time watch a film loop through a peephole; the first parlor opened in New York on April 14, 1894.

facts.text: In February 1888 Muybridge visited Edison's laboratory in West Orange, New Jersey, and proposed combining the zoopraxiscope with the phonograph; Edison did not join him.
In October 1888 Edison filed a caveat for a device to "do for the eye what the phonograph does for the ear", which he called the Kinetoscope.
Edison's assistant W. K. L. Dickson, given the task in 1889, did the bulk of the experimenting, and most modern scholars give him the major credit, though Edison took sole credit.

The Kinetoscope was a wooden cabinet about four feet high; one viewer looked through a peephole at a loop of film about 50 feet long, drawn continuously past a lamp while a spinning shutter let through very brief flashes.
The first Kinetoscope parlor opened in New York on April 14, 1894, with five machines in a row; 25 cents let a customer watch the film in each.

title: Why projection beat the peep show
description: Projecting for a crowd earned more per machine than one-viewer cabinets, so projection overtook the Kinetoscope from 1895; Edison sold Armat and Jenkins's Vitascope as his own in 1896.

facts.text: Edison was slow to develop projection because Kinetoscopes were very profitable, but films projected for large audiences could earn more because fewer machines were needed for the number of viewers.
Projected motion pictures began to overtake Kinetoscope peep shows in 1895.
The Vitascope projector, invented by Thomas Armat and C. Francis Jenkins but marketed as an Edison invention, had its first theatrical showing in New York on April 23, 1896.

title: The Lumières' 1895 Paris screening
description: On December 28, 1895, the Lumières projected short everyday-life films for a paying audience at the Grand Café in Paris, usually counted as cinema's birth; their light three-in-one Cinématographe traveled the world.

facts.text: On December 28, 1895, the Lumière brothers held a showing at the Grand Café on the boulevard des Capucines in Paris, which Britannica calls the beginning of cinema history.
Before the commercial premiere of December 28, 1895, the Lumières had shown their Cinématographe at demonstrations, the first for a small audience in Paris on March 22, 1895.
Woodville Latham's Eidoloscope projector was presented publicly in New York in April 1895.
The Lumières' work began after their father, Antoine, saw Edison's Kinetoscope in Paris in 1894; they aimed to show moving pictures to an audience rather than to one viewer at a time.
The Cinématographe weighed under 5 kg and combined the jobs of camera, printer and projector, which made it easy for operators to travel.
The Lumières' first films recorded everyday French life, such as workers leaving the Lumière factory and a train arriving at a station.
Beginning in 1896 the Lumières sent trained cameraman-projectionists to cities around the world to show films and shoot new ones.

title: The train panic is a legend
description: No reports from the time show audiences fleeing the Lumières' arriving-train film; historian Martin Loiperdinger calls the tale cinema's founding myth.

facts.text: The story that audiences panicked at the Lumières' film of an arriving train has no support in reports from the time; historian Martin Loiperdinger calls the panic legend cinema's founding myth.

title: Méliès and the stop trick
description: Stage magician Georges Méliès saw the Lumière show and turned the camera into a magic box, using the stop trick (stop, change the scene, restart), which Edison's company had used in 1895.

facts.text: Georges Méliès, a stage magician, owned the Théâtre Robert-Houdin in Paris from 1888.
In December 1895, Méliès, then running the Théâtre Robert-Houdin, saw the Lumière Cinématographe demonstrated in Paris.
By Méliès's own account, his camera jammed while he was filming in the Place de l'Opéra, and when he projected the film a bus seemed to turn into a hearse: the stop trick, or substitution splice.
Edison's company had already used the trick in 1895: filming The Execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, it stopped the camera, replaced the actor with a dummy, and resumed filming.
Méliès's films used stop motion, slow motion, dissolves, fade-outs, superimposition and double exposure.
Méliès built a glass-walled film studio at Montreuil, near Paris.

title: A Trip to the Moon
description: Méliès's 1902 A Trip to the Moon, loosely from Jules Verne, used stop motion and superimposition, reached audiences internationally and helped make story films mainstream.

facts.text: A Trip to the Moon (1902), loosely adapted from Jules Verne, runs about 14 minutes and includes the spacecraft striking the man in the moon in the eye.
In A Trip to the Moon, Méliès used camera tricks such as stop motion and superimposition to create fantasy.
A Trip to the Moon was one of the first films to achieve international distribution and helped establish story films as a mainstream product.

title: The Great Train Robbery tells a story across places
description: Porter's 1903 film for Edison's company used 14 shots and cut between the telegraph operator and the bandits to show simultaneous action, a break from theater-like staging.

facts.text: The Great Train Robbery (1903) was made by Edwin S. Porter for Thomas Edison's company and runs about 12 minutes.
The film is built from 14 separate shots: bandits overpower a telegraph operator, rob a train's mail car and passengers, and are chased by a posse.
Porter cut back and forth between the tied-up telegraph operator and the bandits on the train to show action happening at the same time in different places.
Britannica describes the film as a dramatic departure from the front-facing, theatrical staging of its day, establishing continuity of action from shot to shot.

title: The Great Train Robbery on location and on screen
description: Shot in November 1903 in Edison's New York studio and on location in New Jersey, the film ends or opens with an outlaw firing at the camera and helped make the Western a staple.

facts.text: The Great Train Robbery was filmed in November 1903 at Edison's New York studio and on location in New Jersey, including along the Lackawanna Railroad.
In a close-up, the outlaw leader, played by Justus D. Barnes, fires his pistol straight at the camera; exhibitors could show it at the beginning or the end of the film.
The film's success tapped into fascination with the Old West and helped make the Western a staple of American film.

title: Intermittent movement: stop, show, pull
description: A projector advances film one frame at a time and holds each frame still while it is shown; claws or a Maltese cross do the pulling.

facts.text: Intermittent movement advances film one frame at a time, with stationary periods in between, so each frame stands still while it is exposed or shown.
In cameras, the intermittent is typically a claw mechanism that pulls the film down by its sprocket holes.
The four-slot Maltese cross, or Geneva movement, introduced in the 1890s, stops each frame of the moving film in front of the projector's picture aperture.
The Lumière Cinématographe worked like a sewing machine, moving film then holding it still: a cam drove claws through the film's perforations, and two turns of the crank a second advanced 16 frames.

title: The shutter hides the pull and beats flicker
description: A rotating shutter blocks the light while each frame is pulled down, and a twin-bladed shutter flashes each frame twice (48 flashes at 24 fps) to prevent flicker.

facts.text: A rotating shutter blocks the light while the film is pulled down to the next frame, so the movement is never seen.
Flicker happens when images are not flashed quickly enough for the viewer to see the light as continuously on.
Film projectors generally use a twin-bladed shutter that flashes each frame twice, so a film shown at 24 frames per second gives 48 flashes per second.

title: Films saved as paper prints
description: To register copyright, Edison's company and others deposited films at the Library of Congress as photographic prints on paper, which now form its Paper Print Collection.

facts.text: Film companies often copied each other's films, so from October 1896 the Edison Company regularly registered films for copyright, sending them to the Library of Congress as positive photographic prints on paper rolls.
These paper prints, with those from other companies, form the Library of Congress's Paper Print Collection.
The earliest surviving copyrighted film, Edison Kinetoscopic Record of a Sneeze, January 7, 1894, was deposited as a series of photographic prints, not on film.
The Library of Congress holds The Great Train Robbery in its Paper Print Collection.
